screens.heading: That fresh smell
screens.body: After rain, the air sometimes smells clean and earthy. People love that smell. It even has a name: petrichor. Say it like this: PET-ri-kor. Pretty cool, right?

screens.heading: Dry ground waits
screens.body: Before rain falls, the ground can be dry and dusty. Tiny bits of soil and plants sit on the surface. They wait quietly — until raindrops arrive.

screens.heading: Tiny helpers in soil
screens.body: Soil holds tiny living things called bacteria. Some of them make an oil that soaks into the ground. The oil can sit there for a long time without you noticing.

screens.heading: Raindrops splash up
screens.body: When a raindrop hits the ground, it splashes. That splash sends tiny droplets into the air. Those droplets carry the oil smell upward — right to your nose.

screens.heading: Wind brings it to you
screens.body: A little breeze can carry the smell across a yard or street. That is why you sometimes smell rain even before you get wet. Your nose catches it first.

screens.heading: Notice next time
screens.body: Next time it rains, pause for ten seconds. Breathe in slowly. Can you smell petrichor? You are noticing real science — just like a curious explorer.
